Surah al-Qari'ah (The Striking Calamity)

Meccan, and its verses are eleven.

﴿The Striking Calamity﴾. Al-qar‘: it is striking with force and firm impact, such that a loud sound results from it. It is the Resurrection (al-qiyamah), whose beginning is the first blast of the Trumpet and whose end is the decisive judgment between the creatures, as has passed in Surah al-Takwir. It was named so because it strikes hearts and ears with all kinds of terror and horror, and it brings all the upper and lower celestial bodies from one state to another: the sky by splitting and cleaving, the sun and stars by being folded up, dimmed and scattered, the earth by quaking and being changed, and the mountains by being crushed and blown away. And it (al-qari'ah) is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate (khabar) is the words of the Exalted: *

﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ This is on the reading that "mā" (the interrogative "what") is the predicate (khabar) and "al-qāri'ah" (the Striking Calamity) is the subject (mubtada'), not the reverse, because it has been stated more than once that the locus of the benefit (maḥall al-fā'idah) is the predicate, not the subject. There is no doubt that the basis for conveying awe and grandeur here is the expression "mā al-qāri'ah" — "what a wondrous thing it is in its magnitude and dreadfulness." The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun for the sake of emphasizing the terror.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 101, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?﴾ is an emphasis on its terror and dreadfulness, by stating that it lies outside the sphere of created knowledge, in the sense that its greatness is such that the comprehension of anyone scarcely attains it until He makes you know of it. The "mā" is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and "adrāka" is the predicate (khabar), and there is no way to reverse this here. And "mā al-qāri'ah" is a clause which, as has passed, has a place in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khāfid), because adrā (to make know) transitively takes its second object with the preposition "bi," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor would He have made you know of it﴾. So when the interrogative clause came as a suspending element (mu'allaqah) for it, it occupied the position of its second object. The great clause is conjoined to what precedes it of the clause that is the predicate of the first subject, meaning: "And what knowledge has informed you what the matter of the Striking Calamity is?" Since this indicates the gracious promise of informing you of it, He fulfilled that by His saying, exalted is He: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 101, verse 4:

﴿On the Day when mankind will be like scattered moths﴾ — [It is said that] "yawma" (the day) is in the nominative case, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and its vowel is a fatha because it is attached to a verb, even though the verb is imperfect (muḍāri'), as is the view of the Kufans. That is: "It is a day in which mankind will be, in their multitude and dispersion, and in their weakness, humiliation, and confusion, and in their rushing toward the caller like the rushing of moths into the fire." Or it is in the accusative case, governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said, after the affair of al-Qari'ah had been magnified and made to excite curiosity about it for the one upon whom be blessings and peace, to know it: "Remember the day when mankind will be..." etc., for "what will make you know what it is?" And it has been said: it is an adverbial of time whose governing element is an implied verb indicated by al-Qari'ah, i.e., "it (al-Qari'ah) will strike on the day when mankind will be..." etc. And it has been said: its implied construction is "al-Qari'ah will come upon you on the day when it will be..." etc.

And the mountains will be like carded tufts of wool, of various colours, scattered in their parts and flying through the air, as His words, may He be exalted, express: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass by like the passing of clouds﴾. Both of these conditions are among the effects of the Striking Calamity after the second blast, at the gathering of creation. God, Mighty and Majestic, will change the earth into other than the earth and alter its forms, and will set the mountains moving from their places in the terrifying forms mentioned, so that the people of the Gathering may witness them. Although they are crushed and split apart at the first blast, their being set in motion and the leveling of the earth occur only after the second blast, as His words express: ﴿They ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾, ﴿and He will leave it a level plain﴾, ﴿you will not see in it any crookedness or unevenness﴾, ﴿on that Day they will follow the summoner﴾, and His words: ﴿The Day the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾. The following of the summoner, who is Israfil, peace be upon him, and the coming forth of creation before God, glorified be He, can only occur after the resurrection, with certainty. The full discussion has already passed in the commentary on Surah al-Naml.

And the saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Then as for him whose scales are heavy﴾ ...etc., is a general statement of the division of people into two groups, and an indication of the specific states of each of them after the explanation of the states that encompass all people. The "mawazin" (scales) is either the plural of "mawzun" (that which is weighed), meaning the deed that has weight and value before God, as al-Farra' said, or the plural of "mizan" (scale). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is a scale that has a tongue and two pans, in which only deeds are weighed. They said: the pages of deeds are placed in it, and the creatures look at it, to show its justice and to cut off excuses. It was also said: the weighing is an expression for a sound judgment and a just ruling. This was the view of Mujahid, al-A'mash and al-Dahhak, and many of the later scholars chose it. They said: the scale is only used to know the quantities of bodies, so how can the quantities of deeds, which are transient accidents ('a'rad), be known by it? It was also said: the deeds that are apparent in this world appear in the next world in a substantial form (jawhariyya) that corresponds to them in goodness and ugliness. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that good deeds are brought in beautiful forms, and evil deeds in ugly forms, and they are placed in the scale, i.e., whoever's good deeds' quantities outweigh.

Surah 101 (al-Qari'ah), verse 7:

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾ i.e., one that has contentment (in it), or one that is pleasing (to its possessor).
﴿But as for him whose scales are light﴾, meaning: he has no good deed that counts for anything, or his evil deeds outweigh his good deeds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 101, verse 9:

﴿Then his mother⁠ ﴾ means: then his abode (fa-ma'wahu).

﴿Hawiyah⁠﴾ is one of the names of the Fire. It was so named because of the extreme depth of its bottom and the length of its fall. It is narrated that the people of the Fire will keep falling into it for seventy autumns. It was also said that it is the name of the lowest gate of it. He expressed the abode with the letter lam (in the phrase "fa-ummuhu," "his mother") because its inhabitants take refuge in it just as a child takes refuge in its mother. And it is related from Qatadah, 'Ikrimah and al-Kalbi that the meaning is: "the mother of his head is Hawiyah, at the bottom of Jahannam," because he will be thrown into it upside down. The first view is the more fitting one, in agreement with the words of the Most High:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 101, verses 10–11:**

﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾ ﴿A blazing fire.﴾ This is a confirmation (*taqrir*) of it after its vagueness, and an indication that it goes beyond the familiar limits, for glorification and awe. "*Hiya*" is a pronoun referring to *al-Hawiyah*. The final "*ha*" (*ha' al-sakt*, the pausal "h") is for pause. When the reader connects the words, he omits it. It was said: it should not be run on (*idraj*, continuous recitation without pause), lest running on drop it, because it is written in the *mushaf* (the written copy of the Qur'an). Its retention with connection has been permitted.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Qari'ah, Allah the Exalted will make his scale heavy with it on the Day of Resurrection."
